meta.title: Who really said "There are some ideas so absurd that only an intellectual could believe them"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Orwell’s idea, but not his words. In 1945 he wrote “no ordinary man could be such a fool.” The tidy “absurd/intellectual” wording is a later paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There are some ideas so absurd that only an intellectual could believe them'?
meta.ogDescription: Orwell’s thought, but a paraphrase of his words. His 1945 line was “no ordinary man could be such a fool.”

answer.label: Not Orwell’s words — a later paraphrase
answer.authorDates: 1903–1950 · English novelist, essayist & critic (pen name of Eric Arthur Blair)
answer.sourceLine: The idea is genuinely Orwell’s, but this is not what he wrote. In “Notes on Nationalism” (1945) he wrote, “One has to belong to the intelligentsia to believe things like that: no ordinary man could be such a fool.” The neat “so absurd that only an intellectual could believe them” wording is a later paraphrase that appears in none of his works; its closest phrased cousin is a 1959 line by Bertrand Russell ↗.

source.heading: The real source of the thought

docMeta.dd: “no ordinary man could be such a fool” — not “only an intellectual could believe them”

source.excerpt: I have heard it confidently stated, for instance, that the American troops had been brought to Europe not to fight the Germans but to crush an English revolution. One has to belong to the intelligentsia to believe things like that: no ordinary man could be such a fool.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the saying and concludes the “absurd / only an intellectual” phrasing is a paraphrase, not Orwell’s words, with the nearest match a 1959 line by Bertrand Russell: One Has To Belong To the Intelligentsia… ↗.

The primary text of “Notes on Nationalism” contains only “One has to belong to the intelligentsia to believe things like that: no ordinary man could be such a fool ↗” — the word ‘intellectual’ and ‘absurd’ never appear together as popularly quoted.

Per Quote Investigator, paraphrased versions were pinned on Orwell across the decades — by writers including John Podhoretz, Robert Byrne and Thomas Sowell ↗ — hardening a paraphrase into a fake ‘quotation.’
source.excerptNote: Orwell’s actual sentence from “Notes on Nationalism” (1945). The widely shared “so absurd that only an intellectual could believe them” is a later compression of this idea, not a quotation.

source.rightsNote: The thought comes from Orwell’s “Notes on Nationalism” (first published 1945), which remains in copyright in the United States (work published after 1930; author died 1950) — controlled by the Estate of the late Sonia Brownell Orwell. But the exact popular wording appears in no identifiable published work by Orwell or anyone else; as an anonymous paraphrase it has no sourceable rights status of its own, so we classify it as uncertain rather than assert a public-domain claim.

author.bio: George Orwell (Eric Arthur Blair, 1903–1950) was an English novelist and essayist, author of Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four, and a relentless critic of the ideological self-deception he saw in the intelligentsia of his day.

misattribution.heading: The misquote, untangled
misattribution.intro: This is one of those quotes that is ‘right’ in spirit and wrong in fact. Orwell really did skewer intellectuals who believe things no ordinary person would — but he never wrote the neat sentence now stamped on his name.

items.why: “There are some ideas so absurd that only an intellectual could believe them” appears in none of Orwell’s essays, letters or books. Quote Investigator finds it is a later paraphrase ↗ that accreted around his real 1945 remark.

The “so absurd… only very learned men” construction that the modern wording echoes was actually written by Bertrand Russell ↗: “This is one of those views which are so absurd that only very learned men could possibly adopt them.”

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Orwell’s; the wording is not. What he actually wrote in 1945 was “One has to belong to the intelligentsia to believe things like that: no ordinary man could be such a fool ↗.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Orwell wrote “Notes on Nationalism” in the closing months of the Second World War, arguing that intellectuals, more than ordinary people, were prone to swallow whatever their political loyalties required — even when the ‘plainest facts’ contradicted them. The famous jab about intellectuals believing absurdities is a distillation of that argument.

The paraphrase endures because it is punchier than the original and flatters the reader’s common sense. But its very success has buried Orwell’s actual, sharper sentence — a small irony for the essayist who warned that language could be used to make lies sound truthful.
context.pull: The thought is Orwell’s; the polished sentence is somebody else’s.
